text: ULAN BATOR -- Mongolia has suffered estimated damage of about 3.35 trillion Mongolian tugriks (around 928 million U.S. dollars) from a massive wildfire in the eastern province of Dornod, allegedly sparked by a convoy operated by a Japanese-invested company, the country's Minister of Environment and Climate Change Tsend Sandag-Ochir said Wednesday.

Sandag-Ochir announced the preliminary damage assessment at a regular government meeting. The wildfire broke out on Oct. 8 in the core zone of the Numrug Strictly Protected Area in Khalkh Gol soum, an administrative subdivision of Dornod Province. (Mongolia-Japan-Fire)
JAKARTA -- Nine miners were found dead inside a flooded mining pit in Indonesia's West Java province on Wednesday, with 17 others still missing underground, local authorities said in a statement.
The victims were evacuated from two mining tunnels, with six bodies recovered from Tunnel A and three from Tunnel B as of 7 p.m. local time. (Indonesia-Mine-Flood)

Pak Hyon Su, director general of the European Department of the DPRK Foreign Ministry, summoned Sylvain Astier, head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office, and handed him a memorandum from the ministry, urging the office's closure and requiring him to leave the country, said the report. items.title: Hamas security official killed in Israeli airstrike on Gaza City
text: A Palestinian inspects damages following an Israeli airstrike on a residential apartment in western Gaza City, on Nov. 25, 2026. A senior official of the Hamas-run internal security service was killed along with his wife and two daughters in an Israeli airstrike on an apartment in Gaza City early Wednesday, according to Palestinian and medical sources. Palestinian sources said an Israeli drone fired at least one missile at an apartment in Al-Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, setting the unit ablaze. (Photo by Rizek Abdeljawad/Xinhua)

GAZA, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- A senior official of the Hamas-run internal security service was killed along with his wife and two daughters in an Israeli airstrike on an apartment in Gaza City early Wednesday, according to Palestinian and medical sources.
Palestinian sources said an Israeli drone fired at least one missile at an apartment in Al-Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, setting the unit ablaze.
Medical sources told Xinhua that four people were killed in the strike, and their bodies were taken to Al-Shifa Medical Complex in Gaza City.

In a statement, the Hamas-run interior authorities identified the victims as Colonel Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, director of the internal security service in the North Gaza Governorate; his wife, Noura Abu al-Ouf, 41; and their two daughters aged 15 and 13.

It condemned the attack as a "heinous crime and massacre against civilians," adding that the strike was part of ongoing efforts to undermine the security apparatus in the Gaza Strip and sow chaos in Palestinian society.
The Israeli army has not commented on the reported killing of Abu al-Ouf.
The strike came one day after Naim Abu Nahal, head of the Hamas-run internal security service, was killed in an Israeli airstrike west of Gaza City. ■

items.title: China's Shenzhou-24 spaceship docks with Tiangong space station
text: This real-time image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on Nov. 25, 2026 shows China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship docking with the Tiangong space station. China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship successfully docked with the Tiangong space station at 11:56 a.m. (Beijing Time) on Wednesday, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). The spaceship made a fast, automated rendezvous and docking with the front port of Tiangong's core module Tianhe. The whole docking process took approximately 3.5 hours, said the CMSA. The astronaut trio aboard the spaceship, which comprises Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to visit Tiangong, will then enter the Tianhe module. The Shenzhou-23 crew members in the space station are ready to receive the new arrivals. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang)

JIUQUAN, Nov. 25 (Xinhua) -- China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship successfully docked with the Tiangong space station at 11:56 a.m. (Beijing Time) on Wednesday, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA).
The spaceship made a fast, automated rendezvous and docking with the front port of Tiangong's core module Tianhe. The whole docking process took approximately 3.5 hours, said the CMSA.

The astronaut trio aboard the spaceship, which comprises Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to visit Tiangong, will then enter the Tianhe module. The Shenzhou-23 crew members in the space station are ready to receive the new arrivals.
The spaceship, atop a Long March-2F carrier rocket, blasted off at 8:18 a.m. (Beijing Time) from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China on Wednesday. ■

items.title: Chinese women's history is being rediscovered
text: On Nov 21, Guangxi Normal University Press hosted the 2026 Annual Academic Publishing Forum in Guilin, Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region.

The forum, themed "Reassessing the History of Chinese Women", focused on topics such as women's public culture, gender and emotional order, and women in the court and grassroots settings. It aimed to engage both online and offline audiences in returning to historical contexts to understand women's real situations in labor, expression, physicality, and the rule of law.

Inaugurated in October 2023, this forum has successively focused on Song Dynasty (960-1279), Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties, and urban history, inviting renowned scholars and engaging nearly 200,000 readers online and offline to explore historical details.

In recent years, the study of Chinese women's history has transitioned from "forgotten" to "rediscovery". However, in the public's perception, it often remains stuck in a simplistic "oppression-liberation" narrative, and women's presence in history is frequently reduced to a few stereotypical images, said Liu Longjin, head of the Academics brand at Guangxi Normal University Press.

The Academics series has released books, including Women's Sports in Modern Eastern China: 1895-1937 by Taiwan scholar Yu Chien-ming; Reproducing Women: Medicine, Metaphor and Childbirth in Late Imperial China by scholar Yi-Li Wu; The Rise of Female Narrative in Early Modern China by Taiwan scholar Hu Siao-chen; Ming Ruo Zhao Shuang (Life Like Morning Frost): Law, Society and Women in Dream of the Red Chamber by Ke Lan, a law professor from Huazhong University of Science and Technology; and Women Playing Men: Yue Opera and Social Change in Twentieth-century Shanghai by Jiang Jin, a professor from East China Normal University.
These works aim to present a more nuanced and vivid portrayal of women's history through interdisciplinary perspectives and detailed micro-narratives.
At the opening ceremony, Guangxi Normal University Press signed publishing agreements with scholars Ke Lan and Xu Ning.
"Academic research and publishing carry the mission of continuing knowledge, spreading ideas, and conveying values," said Huang Xuanzhuang, president of Guangxi Normal University Press Group.

Over the past four years, the university press has continuously deepened the interaction between the publishing and academic worlds. With this forum as a new starting point, the publisher hopes to strengthen ties between academia and publishing, facilitate communication between scholars and readers, and jointly build a community of shared destiny in academic research and publishing, Huang added.

During the forum, Mao Liping, a professor of history at Renmin University of China, said what impressed her most about the "Uncovering Her, Reflecting Me" interview project was how scholars systematically broke down stereotypes about women, showing that women are "not all of the one type". Participants in this forum ranged from those born in the 1950s to the 1990s.
"Women from different age groups tell the life stories of historical women, which are also our own life stories," she said.

items.title: Media key to boosting Sino-Russian ties
text: The media is playing a vital role in promoting cultural and business exchanges between Russia and China, media professionals from the two countries said on Wednesday.

Alexey Urazov, director of International Cooperation and Special Projects at Russia's National Media Group, said the task of the media today is not merely to talk about Russia and China, but to tell stories of the two countries together.

"Diplomacy opens doors for business and creates opportunities, while the media helps millions of people make use of those opportunities," he said at the seventh China-Russia Media Forum in Moscow, which was co-hosted by news agencies TASS and Xinhua.

Trade and commerce, according to Urazov, have found a natural ally in the press. Cross-border e-commerce, investment road shows and industrial matchmaking are increasingly packaged in stories and programs that make distant markets seem more accessible. Regular content exchanges between Russian and Chinese media outlets are building what he called a "shared information space" that shortens the distance for readers on both sides.

Alexey Yefimov, general director of Channel One Worldwide, noted that his company has spent nearly a decade as the first Russian television company to broadcast in Chinese, with its Katyusha channel airing more than 9,000 programs as a "television window" into Russia for millions of Chinese viewers.
The bilingual channel, he said, also carries an educational function, helping audiences in both countries sharpen their language skills while sparking curiosity about travel.

Urazov pointed to the joint feature "Red Silk" and its forthcoming sequel — coproduced by Russian and Chinese teams and already licensed in 48 countries — as proof that films can work as cultural diplomacy.

Huang Mei, dean of the School of Russian Studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, said that language and translation are a "school of empathy", helping Chinese readers reach Russia's classics while Russian readers discover Chinese works.
Alexey Goreslavsky, director general of the Institute for Internet Development, called for pairing Russian and Chinese presenters to introduce each other's cities.
With some 60,000 Chinese students studying in Russia, he said, young musicians, designers and game developers are emerging as a new generation of cultural ambassadors.
Artificial intelligence was another defining new theme of the forum. Delegates discussed using AI to identify and trace disinformation.
Fresh cooperation documents were inked between Chinese and Russian news organizations, among them a memorandum of cooperation between China Daily and TASS.

text: Ya'nan, a giant panda at a wildlife park in Qinhuangdao, Hebei province, has once again charmed residents: this time with a playful tree-climbing spree.

items.title: Xi, Pakistani president exchange congratulations over joint spaceflight mission
text: BEIJING -- President Xi Jinping said on Wednesday that the joint space exploration by astronauts from China and Pakistan is a vivid embodiment of the deep-rooted friendship between the two countries.
It marks another important achievement in bilateral cooperation, Xi said while exchanging congratulations with Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari on the joint spaceflight mission.

In the message, Xi said that he was glad to learn of a Pakistani astronaut's successful entry into space aboard a Chinese Shenzhou spaceship for the first time, making him the first foreign astronaut to inhabit China's space station.
Xi extended his warm congratulations to the Pakistani government and people, as well as to astronauts and space professionals from both countries on behalf of the Chinese government and people.

Xi noted that China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners, saying that the friendship between the two countries has remained rock-solid and unbreakable since diplomatic ties were established 75 years ago.

Emphasizing that China's space station is an ark of peace, friendship and cooperation, Xi said that China stands ready to work with Pakistan and other countries to advance the peaceful use of outer space, deepen international space cooperation, and improve global governance in outer space, to ensure that outer space exploration delivers greater benefits to the humanity.
For his part, Zardari expressed profound appreciation to the Chinese government and the brotherly Chinese people on behalf of the Pakistani government and people.

He said the historic space cooperation between Pakistan and China and the first Pakistani astronaut entering China's space station come as the two countries commemorate the 75th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations.

Such cooperation demonstrates China's remarkable progress in space science and technology, its firm commitment to the peaceful use of outer space, and the significance of building a community with a shared future for humanity, Zardari said, adding that it will further strengthen bilateral friendship, and promote the all-weather strategic cooperative partnership between the two countries to a higher level.

items.title: China extradites economic crime suspect from Russia
text: A suspect surnamed Shu was recently extradited from Russia to China in connection with a case involving more than 15 billion yuan ($2.25 billion) in allegedly illegal absorption of public deposits, the Ministry of Public Security said on Wednesday.
The extradition followed efforts by Chinese police, with assistance from the Chinese Embassy in Russia, the ministry said.

Shu allegedly solicited deposits from the public by promoting fictitious wealth management products and promising high annual returns, despite lacking approval from financial regulators and the qualifications required to accept public deposits.
Police in Yinzhou district of Ningbo, Zhejiang province, launched an investigation into Shu in October 2024.

Prosecutors approved his arrest in February 2025 on suspicion of illegally taking deposits from the public. Russian police apprehended Shu in November that year, prompting Chinese authorities to submit an extradition request.
Russia approved the request in September 2026, and Shu was extradited to China on Nov 5.

An official with the ministry's economic crime investigation bureau said the extradition demonstrated the determination of China and Russia to jointly combat crime and marked a milestone in deepening bilateral law enforcement and judicial cooperation.

Chinese police will continue to strengthen international law enforcement cooperation, bring fugitive criminal suspects to justice and protect the lawful rights and interests of the public, the official added.

items.title: Weekly train service linking China, Mongolia and Russia launched
text: A passenger train departed Beijing for Irkutsk, Russia, on Wednesday morning, marking the launch of a weekly rail service linking China, Mongolia and Russia.
The V3 train left Beijing Railway Station at 7:27 am and is scheduled to arrive in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, on Thursday afternoon before reaching Irkutsk on Friday afternoon.
The 2,666-kilometer journey takes about 55 hours. The train stops at cities and towns in all three countries, including Jining and Ereenhot in China, Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia and Ulan-Ude in Russia.

items.title: Shenzhou mission to conduct 90 sci-tech space tests
text: The Shenzhou XXIV mission will carry out 90 scientific experiments and technological tests aboard the Tiangong space station, the China Manned Space Agency announced on Tuesday.

The experiments and tests will cover space life sciences, space materials science, microgravity fluid physics and combustion science, fundamental physics, space medicine, and cutting-edge aerospace technologies, said Zhang Jingbo, a senior engineer and spokesman for the agency, during a news conference held at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China.

As part of space life science experiments, the crew will build vascular organ chips and multi-type organ-on-a-chip devices to study how the space environment affects key physiological processes such as vascular aging, aiming to develop new strategies for preventing and treating age-related conditions, he said.

Zhang noted that the Shenzhou XXIII crewmembers have already made significant findings in this field. Their multi-omics research has revealed that spaceflight reduces the differentiation efficiency of human-induced primordial germ cells by about 50 percent, he said.

It has also identified the key pathways through which germ cells adapt to space conditions, including extracellular matrix regulation, cytoskeleton remodeling, translation control and lipid metabolism, he added.

In space materials science research, the Shenzhou XXIV astronauts will focus on the in-orbit fabrication and performance control of ultrahigh-temperature niobium-silicon intermetallic compounds and calcium-silicon multicomponent bioglass, as well as scientific studies of monocrystalline silicon and perovskite materials, Zhang said.

He noted that the Shenzhou XXIII mission produced China's first millimeter-scale deep-ultraviolet nonlinear optical crystal — potassium beryllium fluoroborate — aboard the space station. The microgravity environment significantly improved the crystal's growth quality, laying an important material foundation for high-power deep-ultraviolet laser devices.

In the field of space medicine, experiments under the Space Human Research Program will continue, Zhang said. The program will include mining multi-omics data to map the human spaceflight multi-omics atlas, quantify changes in behavioral capabilities during long-haul missions, and explore the mechanisms underlying brain function, he said.

Zhang noted that the Shenzhou XXIII astronauts have introduced advanced detection technologies, including continuous muscle imaging and intelligent quantitative assessment, in-orbit detection of multiple proteins from trace amounts of whole blood, and an AI-powered multimodal exercise-load evaluation model.
These technologies enable noncontact physiological monitoring and objective fatigue assessment, he added.

In the field of aerospace technology, the Shenzhou XXIV mission will test key technologies for a chemical-electric hybrid propulsion system featuring multiple operating modes and novel ionic liquid propellants.

items.title: A Spanish Photographer in Shanghai: Capturing the Moments That Make a Family
text: For Spanish photographer Nuria Sánchez, family photography is about preserving the moments that matter most. Born in Málaga, on Spain's southern coast, she has made Shanghai her home for the past 11 years, building a practice focused on families, maternity and weddings.

Her path to photography began in childhood, led her through a career in human resources, and eventually brought her back to the work she loves. Today, she hopes to offer families in Shanghai a more natural, relaxed and spontaneous approach to photography – one that captures not just how a family looks, but the memories they make together.
Born in Málaga, on Spain's southern coast, Nuria Sánchez has made Shanghai her home for the past 11 years, building a practice focused on families, maternity and weddings. Andrea Martinez
Before we talk about business, would you please introduce yourself?

I don't remember exactly when my passion for photography began, but it must have been at a very young age. On the day of my First Communion, when I was nine, I received four cameras as gifts. It seems my relatives and friends had recognized my love of photography before I had fully realized it myself.

At 14, while still in secondary school, I began studying photography. I became the photographer for my friends, who enjoyed playing the role of models, and some of my pictures were even displayed in the school hallways. Later, I started accompanying other photographers to weddings, earning a little money while doing something I loved. I often preferred that to going out with my friends.

I eventually completed my studies in human resources and worked as a labor consultant. But I later changed the course of my life and pursued formal training as a higher technician in imaging. My first assignments were documentaries and exhibitions, followed by weddings.

It was after having my own children that I became interested in family photography. I wanted to keep them little forever and preserve those fleeting moments, because children grow up so quickly. Many of my wedding clients also had children or were expecting, and that's how I began working in maternity and family photography.
It was after having her own children that Nuria became interested in family photography. She wanted to keep them little forever and preserve those fleeting moments. Andrea Martinez
Why did you decide to strike out on your own to build up a business?

When I first arrived in China, I spent the first two years settling my family into our new life and getting to know the city, its culture and language. Once everything had fallen into place, however, my passion for photography drew me back to work, and I felt more eager than ever to pursue it in Shanghai.
Nuria captures an intimate moment of everyday family life on the streets of Shanghai. Courtesy of Nuria Sánchez

items.title: Uncovering the Terracotta Army’s Stunning Hidden Artistry
text: When glimpsing the Terracotta Army for the first time, almost everyone is awestruck by its sheer scale: thousands of armored clay figures standing in perfect formation, their gray earthen bodies stretching rank upon rank. At first glance, the ghostly 2,000-year-old soldiers look as if they were cast from a single mold.

But look closer, and the impression of uniformity begins to dissolve. No two faces are exactly alike: brows thick or faint, eyes wide open or slightly narrowed, cheekbones high or low, jawlines rounded or square. When viewed individually, each warrior is far more than a figure: it is a work of art as intricate as many Renaissance statues.

Zhao Hui (Steve Zhao) has spent much of the past 25 years trying to capture this hidden artistry. A veteran photographer who trained under cinematographer Peter Levy in the 1980s, Zhao became well known for his portraiture. His 1996 project “China Story” has toured more than 30 countries.
Zhao Hui (Steve Zhao) poses for a photo at the Emperor Qinshihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum in Xi’an, Shaanxi province. Courtesy of Zhao

Since 2001, he has applied his talent for portrait photography to the Terracotta Army, amassing images of more than 2,000 figures. The works offer a striking new perspective on the warriors, often zooming in close enough to highlight the carved stroke of an eyebrow, the turn of a cheekbone, or even faint fingerprints left in the clay by a Qin dynasty artisan.

For Zhao, the project is also about more than changing perceptions of the Terracotta Army; it’s part of a wider effort to document, classify, and analyze it. The vast photo archive helps researchers understand the production processes, craftsmanship, and organization behind the relics — and, most importantly for Zhao, the anonymous master sculptors who carved them.

In this interview, Sixth Tone sat down with Zhao to discuss how his project began and how it has shaped our understanding of the Terracotta Warriors. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.
Sixth Tone: The Terracotta Army has long been a research focus for archaeologists and historians, but what led you to study them through high-definition photography?
Zhao: At first, it was just a routine assignment. In 2001, the China National Tourism Administration approached me to photograph the Terracotta Warriors. It was a rare opportunity, of course.

My task was to capture the warriors in the finest possible detail. That is far harder than most people imagine: heritage photography is not simply pointing a lens at an object. Every click of the shutter is a repeated negotiation with light, angle, material, and patience. The warriors are massive and their preservation conditions special, so every shoot requires meticulous preparation and on-site coordination.

After taking enough high-definition images, I began to notice striking details — the rise and fall of a brow ridge, the hooked line at the corner of an eye, the marks left by the sculptors’ hands. Perhaps it’s because I’m a portrait photographer, trained to observe people.

items.title: Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019331/Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
text: Amid nationwide classroom phone bans, “paper short dramas,” half-meter-long printouts of scenes from short dramas folded into the shape of a smartphone, have recently surged in popularity among Chinese primary school students.

“The CEO’s Runaway Sweetheart,” “Reborn as the Heiress of a Tycoon,” and “The School Bully Forces Me to Date Him” are just a few examples of the stories now stocked by school-adjacent stores and e-commerce platforms, selling for as little as 1 yuan ($0.14), domestic media reported Monday.

In 2021, China’s Ministry of Education issued a notice stating that primary and secondary school students should not bring phones into the classroom, and any phone brought to school must be kept by the school. The ministry tightened this in 2025, banning phones and other electronic devices in school classrooms as part of a student mental health initiative.
Paper short dramas’ accordion-style design allow them to be easily concealed and taken into school. They typically contain scenes from multiple episodes, pairing screenshots with written dialogue.

Despite often containing adult, vulgar, and violent content — in “The CEO’s Runaway Sweetheart,” for instance, a female character sleeps with a legendary CEO and becomes the envy of her peers — paper short dramas are marketed as toys, with some packaging citing toy-safety standards that are outdated or inapplicable to a paper booklet.
This marketing tactic allows sellers, who have not obtained permission from short drama producers to reproduce or distribute the content, to dodge copyright laws.
China’s short drama users reportedly reached nearly 664 million as of December last year. Industry estimates put the potential lost output value due to piracy at as high as 20 billion yuan.

In interviews with domestic media, some parents also reported concerns about the adult content in paper short dramas being available to children with no prior screening, saying that such stories might negatively impact their children’s values.

A hashtag related to paper short dramas on microblogging platform Weibo had garnered over 170 million views as of Thursday. Many commenters called the idea creative, terming it a “new kind of comic strip,” while others criticized it for exposing minors to harmful content.
“Products like this need tight control. Don’t let them poison kids,” one user wrote.
(Header image: A box of different paper short dramas, each shaped like a smartphone. From Weibo)

items.title: The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019319/The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
text: Zhong Weiting’s wife recently bought him a pair of trousers with four front pockets. They’re for the little metal objects he carries around — things that spin, slide, click, or flip open, some made from titanium and costing thousands of yuan.
Each day, he picks a few from a plastic organizer originally bought for socks. He plays with them in elevators, in his car, and at his desk, switching to quieter models when other people are around.

For Zhong, 32, they help relieve stress and keep his restless hands occupied. “I like the sounds they make, and knowing exactly how they’ll respond gives me a sense of certainty,” he tells Sixth Tone. “I feel a kind of electric tingling in my fingertips.”

For all their elaborate mechanisms, they’re just toys to fiddle with. And Zhong, an export salesman in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen who began collecting only in November 2025, already owns 25, including one he bought this month for 2,199 yuan ($330).

Across China, the toys have found a growing following under the name EDC, short for “everyday carry,” a term borrowed from an online subculture centered on practical gear such as pocketknives and flashlights. On social media, they’re also dubbed “cyber walnuts,” after the traditional Chinese pastime of rolling a pair of walnuts in the hand.

Among the most popular designs are sliders, known in China as “push cards,” whose metal plates produce a series of tactile clicks as they slide against each other. Some toys mimic the motion of revealing a playing card or recreate the sharp tap of a telegraph key, with adjustable resistance and sound on more elaborate models.

Basic models sell for less than 100 yuan, while stainless steel versions typically cost 300 to 500 yuan. Limited editions made from rarer metals or featuring elaborate designs can run into the thousands.
Between July 2025 and June 2026, online sales of EDC toys tracked by consulting firm Meritco Databank rose 55.5% to more than 45 million yuan, with nearly 500,000 toys sold, up 78% year on year.

The vast majority of the trade, however, still takes place within collector circles. While a few large brands sell openly on popular e-commerce platforms, smaller makers rely on private groups on Chinese super app WeChat to announce new releases, sometimes limited to just a few dozen pieces.

At an EDC exhibition in Beijing in October, organizer Fu Chunjun told domestic media that the community has a name for its growing obsession: the “men’s version of Pop Mart,” the Chinese collectible-toy company known for its blind boxes.
But when Zhong shows his latest purchases to friends, few understand the appeal. “They think, why should a plastic or stainless steel gadget sell for 500 yuan?” he says.
To buy a toy from one vendor at Shanghai’s EDC exhibition in April, Guo Songhao first had to draw one of two jokers from a deck of 21 playing cards.

He drew the big joker, securing a limited-edition knuckle roller, a small metal toy designed to be rolled and flipped between the fingers. “My luck was pretty good that day,” the 25-year-old Shanghai-based engineer tells Sixth Tone.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019318/A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
text: A Shanghai university is now giving each student and staff member up to 100 million AI tokens a week, saying that it hopes to make tokens a standard teaching resource equal to books, lab equipment, and databases.

University members may use the tokens to access a range of AI models and tools after signing in to the university website with their campus ID, as announced by Shanghai University of Finance and Economics’ (SUFE) official WeChat account on Nov. 21.
Tokens are the smallest pieces of information that AI models can process. Students can use them to debug code, clean data, conduct research, and even build their own AI agents.

China’s daily token consumption hit roughly 500 trillion in June, nearly four times that of December 2025. State-owned telecommunications carriers now sell token plans to consumers, with China Telecom’s cheapest plan costing 9.9 yuan ($1.50) a month for 10 million tokens — a 10th of SUFE’s weekly, per-person limit.
SUFE is the latest Chinese university to provide computing power and free token quotas to students and staff as a public resource, a trend that began earlier this fall.

Starting this September in Beijing, Tsinghua University began offering each student and staff member 1,000 yuan in “computing vouchers,” while Peking University offers a year of free access to Qoder, a cross-LLM AI coding assistant, and 3,000 credits a month. In the central Hunan province, Hunan University students receive 2 million tokens a day. Shanghai’s Tongji University also launched its own plan in October, giving students and faculty 100 million tokens a week.

“In the past, when you’d say a school had good infrastructure, you’d be referring to its gym and library,” Xue Lan, dean of the Institute for AI International Governance at Tsinghua University, told domestic media. “Going forward, computing platforms, LLM data centers, and high-powered internet may be the important infrastructure of schools in the future.”

However, education researchers also report concerns that access to free tokens may fuel “idle teaching,” where teachers create assignments using AI and students submit AI-generated answers, creating a loop in which the work is completed but no real learning takes place.

“Measuring the value of token use is not about how many tokens are actually consumed but what kind of learning they advance in students,” Zhang Duanhong, director of the Center for Educational Policy Research at Tongji University, told domestic media.

items.title: A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
text: “Xiao Ming and his mom and dad are eating out at a restaurant. After they finish eating, his mom wants to take home the leftovers, but his dad thinks it’s unbecoming. What would you do and say if you were Xiao Ming?” poses a Chinese exam question.
“If I were Xiao Ming, I would tell my mom not to pack the leftovers because we have plenty of money, and it would be embarrassing if people saw us doing so,” one student responds.

This answer to a primary school Chinese language exam question has sparked online debate over how schools should balance encouraging children to express their opinions with promoting moral values, with a related hashtag attracting over 46 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

The controversy began when the parent of a third-grader in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, shared a photo of the assignment alongside their child’s answer in a WeChat parent group, which was later leaked, according to domestic media. The child’s teacher marked the answer incorrect, deducting all four potential points. Above, a large red check mark adorns a revised answer written by the student that states: “1) I would pack the leftovers with my family. 2) I would tell my dad that all food is grown through the hard work of farmers, and we shouldn’t waste it just because we’re afraid of losing face.”

Many social media users pointed out the apparent conflict between nurturing critical thinking and penalizing it. “It’s unreasonable to punish students for such answers in a Chinese language exam,” one user wrote. “While it may appear to promote ‘the right values,’ deducting scores as a means of enforcement only teaches children to lie to get what they want.”

Others agreed with the teacher, saying that schools also have a responsibility to help children develop sound values and moral judgment. “(Children) should be encouraged to think outside the box, but their ideas must be grounded in the correct values,” wrote another user.

In recent years, China has sought to curb food waste, enacting the Anti-Food Waste Law in 2021 to cut waste across the food supply chain. In 2020, the Ministry of Education also urged schools to teach frugality and the importance of reducing leftovers. Authorities have also cracked down in recent years on banquets, discouraging excessive food ordering as a display of wealth and generosity.

Zhao Tongwei, a senior teacher and principal of Shanghai-based Shengqiao Central Primary School, told local media that the student’s response reflected a tension between attitudes absorbed from everyday life and the values schools seek to promote.
“Chinese language education is about more than teaching practical skills; it also has a humanistic and educational role. Upholding sound values is a principle that must not be compromised,” he said.

The aim, Zhao said, should be to help students think for themselves. Simply deducting marks could discourage children from expressing what they genuinely believe, he warned, and instead advocate reflection through writing exercises, one-on-one conversations, or whole-class discussions on the topic.
(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

items.title: Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
text: Almost 30 years ago, Carrie Bradshaw opened the TV phenomenon “Sex and the City” with a question: “Why are there so many great unmarried women, and no great unmarried men?” Later, she backs up her assertion with data, declaring that “there are 1.3 million single men in New York, (and) 1.8 million single women.”

Carrie was speaking about turn-of-the-millennium New York, but women in major Chinese cities such as Beijing and Shanghai will have little problem understanding her plight. Marriage rates have declined across the board in recent years, but the drop has been felt most keenly by two very different groups: urban women and rural men.

To get an idea of the problem, take a map of China and color each prefecture-level city red if men there are more likely to be single than women, and blue if the reverse is true. The result is striking. Less developed inland provinces such as Yunnan, Guizhou, and Gansu turn deep red. The country’s richest urban clusters — the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region — turn deep blue. The line between them follows, almost exactly, the line between China’s poorer and wealthier regions.
In other words, China’s cities are full of highly educated single women. In less developed areas, singles are disproportionately men with little education.

China’s skewed sex ratio can explain why there are more single men than single women overall. Yet it cannot fully explain the geographic distribution of single men and women. For its part, media coverage tends to oversimplify the phenomenon as a problem of willingness, with young Chinese rejecting the concept of marriage altogether.

But is that true? Our research, based on two decades of data from national population censuses and the comprehensive China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) surveys, paints a more complete — and complex — picture of how demographic transformation in educational attainment, regional imbalances in skills and industries, and cultural norms have contributed to China’s unbalanced marriage market.

Let’s start with education. Over the past several decades, Chinese women have quietly but quickly caught up with men in educational attainment. Among Chinese born between 1960 and 1995, the education gap between men and women steadily narrowed. For the cohort born around 1985, women college graduates outnumber their male counterparts. And for Chinese born in the mid-1990s or later, the gap in women’s favor is large and continues to widen, especially at the postgraduate level.

This shift coincided with a decisive transformation in China’s economic structure. The services sector, which is disproportionately concentrated in major cities, has grown, drawing women, especially those with degrees, out of agriculture and manufacturing. In 2000, college-educated women were 17 percentage points less likely than college-educated men to work in the services sector; by 2015, they were 21 points more likely to hold such positions.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
text: Chinese archaeologists have announced discoveries from four sites across the country, including Paleolithic campsite ruins and greater details of an aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture.

The findings, announced at a Wednesday conference held by China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration, come from four years of work at four sites along the Yangtze River. They include Taohuahe in the southwestern Sichuan province; Fanshan in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province; Lingtoushang in the eastern Jiangxi province; and Laohudun in the central Hubei province.
The discoveries were presented by Archaeology China, a government program launched in 2018 to fund long-term excavations investigating the origins of farming and civilization.

Taohuahe, discovered in 2022, has yielded over 13,000 Paleolithic-age stone artifacts, including large stone choppers, and 179 animal fossils dating from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, researchers at the conference announced. Excavations have also revealed stone-working and storage areas, cobblestone surfaces, and a semicircular refuse pit.
Wang Youping, an archaeologist at Peking University, told domestic media that, unlike in other archaeological digs in southern China, numerous animal bones have been recovered at Taohuahe.

“Southern China’s acidic soil usually destroys bone,” Wang said. “Researchers had assumed that people in the lush south relied mainly on plants. The (presence of animal) bones suggests that meat was equally important to their work, daily lives, and evolution.”

The second site discussed at the meeting, Fanshan, was discovered 40 years ago and is the highest-ranking aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture ever found, researchers said. The Liangzhu culture, located in northern present-day Hangzhou, flourished about 5,000 years ago. UNESCO added the ruins of its walled city and system of dams and reservoirs to its World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations that began in 2024 indicate that a walled compound enclosed the site’s cemetery mound. At least three buildings stood at its center, including a large oval structure raised on stilts, likely used for ceremonies. The compound lies on a ridge that formed part of the surrounding area’s water system, leading researchers to hypothesize that the tombs, ritual spaces, and dams were planned as a single complex.

After last year’s discovery of a courtyard wall at the Fanshan site, archaeologists uncovered a group of three related buildings this year. Wang said the wall may have formed the cemetery’s outer boundary, while the buildings may have served as sacrificial halls. He added that the culture may already have had a mausoleum system.

Researchers also announced at the conference that they have discovered Neolithic and Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) settlements at a third site, Lingtoushang. The settlements contained evidence of smelting and large quantities of copper, shedding light on close cultural exchange and how the societies exploited and controlled metal resources.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019307/Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
text: For coffee growers in China’s southwestern Yunnan province, Starbucks and Nestlé used to be the only buyers in town. Every harvest season, their purchasing stations would have lines of loaded trucks stretching for days.

Plantation owner Zou Qingquan recalls once waiting a whole week to sell her beans to Nestlé. Back then, she says, the company revised its purchase price twice a week based on changes in the international commodity market, “so your beans were making or losing money as they sat there in the truck.”

Over the past five years, however, these two global giants have been losing their grip on the Yunnan coffee market. Rapid growth among domestic brands such as Seesaw, Manner, Luckin, and the Mixue Group, along with a shift toward specialty coffee, has opened new sales channels for farmers and pushed up prices.

According to the agricultural industry analysis platform Beedata, Nestlé and Starbucks paid an average of 48.09 yuan ($7.20) and 48.18 yuan per kilogram, respectively, for commercial-grade Yunnan green beans in the first quarter of 2026. For Luckin, it was 50.37 yuan.

But while growers’ incomes have risen, some warn that an increasingly indiscriminate buying frenzy, which in some cases is leading to the sale of unripe beans, risks disrupting established trade relationships and negatively affecting the quality and image of Yunnan coffee.

Ma Xiaojin, who manages two coffee-growing cooperatives in Yunnan’s Menglian Dai, Lahu and Va Autonomous County, used to regularly drive the 10 hours from his farm to the Starbucks Farmer Support Center, a training and purchasing facility in central Pu’er, a city arguably best known for its eponymous tea. There, he’d join the line of trucks and wait four or five days to have his beans graded, costing him at least 2,000 yuan in truck rental costs.

Starbucks has exacting quality standards and purchases beans only from growers certified under its Coffee and Farmer Equity (CAFE) Practices program, which in January included 3,400 farms in Yunnan. The American company is also known for paying more for high-quality beans than its Swiss competitor, Nestlé.

“You can’t just show up and expect Starbucks to take your beans,” says Hao Yi, who used to work for Starbucks in coffee production. “They don’t just check each batch; they monitor your quality over several consecutive years. That’s why, in the early days, getting your beans into Starbucks was a source of pride. It also brought your subsequent harvests to the attention of specialty coffee roasters.”

In 2017, Starbucks began selling selected Yunnan beans as part of its high-end Reserve line. For growers, making the cut was no easy feat. If their products passed a preliminary check, they had to provide three large samples from each sack for testing and agree to follow-up screenings.

Specialty beans from Zou’s estate were selected in 2021, with Starbucks offering 48 yuan per kilogram. At the time, her farm was selling to the open market for more than 60 yuan per kilogram. “We earned less, but working with a big brand was good publicity for us, so it was still a net gain,” she says. The following year, many new buyers approached Zou to purchase the same beans.

items.title: China sets new record in deep oil well casing replacement in Xinjiang region
text: The Xinjiang Oilfield, a major oil production base in northwestern China, belonging to the China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) has announced that it has completed a deep underground casing replacement trial at a depth of 1,819 meters, setting a new domestic record and marking progress in technologies designed to repair aging oil wells and extend their service life, the China News Service reported Saturday.

The expanded field trial was recently completed at a Gobi Desert drilling site in the Luliang oilfield, with the operation successfully reconnecting 1,819 meters of casing and completing cementing work in the space between the casing and the surrounding wellbore.

The achievement extends the limits of a technique developed by the oilfield to tackle severe damage to underground well casings, which can otherwise make wells difficult to maintain and continue operating.

In an oil well, steel casing pipes are installed inside the drill hole to support the well walls and provide a stable passage for extracting oil or injecting water. Over years of operation, however, these pipes can corrode, become deformed or break, potentially restricting the well's internal passage and disrupting production.

At the Xinjiang Oilfield, located in the Junggar Basin in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, prolonged exposure to highly mineralized water and the gradual deformation of water-absorbing mudstone formations have contributed to increasingly serious casing damage, including large sections suffering leakage and broken pipes.

Conventional repair methods, such as plugging damaged sections, may only address the immediate leakage without removing the underlying damaged casing. Meanwhile, traditional casing replacement techniques used in shallower sections are not well suited to the complicated conditions encountered deeper underground.

To address the problem, researchers at the Xinjiang Oilfield's Oil Production Technology Research Institute developed a deep open-hole casing replacement technique in 2025. The approach involves removing damaged casing sections and installing replacement pipes, aiming to restore the wellbore to its original internal diameter rather than simply sealing the damaged areas.

An initial field trial was successfully conducted in October 2025 at Well 1424, operated by the Baikouquan Oil Production Plant. The operation replaced casings at a depth of 996 meters and accomplished 809 meters of open-hole casing milling, setting two domestic records at the time.
Building on the experience, the research team continued refining the technique in 2026, focusing on several challenges that had affected the efficiency and safety of deep underground operations.

These included difficulties in milling long unsupported sections of casing, the risk of tools becoming stuck when working along the edge of the casing, and the time-consuming process of cutting and retrieving damaged pipes at greater depths.

items.title: China and Japan hit back at Trump's new tariff plans
China may not have planned Jensen Huang's affair with accused Chinese spy
text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was returned to the job earlier this week, the board reinstating him amidst plummeting stock prices and apparent intervention from President Donald Trump. Now doubt is being cast on allegations that one of Huang's affair partners was a Chinese spy.

Huang has admitted to cheating on his wife with at least four partners as of this week, however his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) has drawn the most scrutiny. A former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, Ms. Huang is suspected of being an intelligent agent who shared information with the Chinese government and smuggled Nvidia chips into China, circumventing U.S. restrictions.

As such, Nvidia opened an independent investigation once Huang and Ms. Huang's relationship came to light, as well as established a committee to oversee the company's national security policies and export control compliance. Huang will also be interviewed by the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee, House Select Committee on China, and House Intelligence Committee on Dec. 1, and testify before the U.S. Senate on Dec. 3.

However, the Wall Street Journal and New York Times now report that the U.S. has no evidence that the Chinese government directed Ms. Huang to begin an affair with Nvidia's CEO. Instead, current evidence indicates that the pair's extramarital entanglement may have been a matter of ordinary human infidelity rather than deliberate international espionage. U.S officials reportedly informed congressional staffers of this in a briefing on Nov. 24, the day after Nvidia reinstated Huang.
        
            The best tech deal this week
                            
                    
    The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

This isn't to say that U.S. agencies didn't find any link between Ms. Huang and the Chinese government at all. U.S. officials reportedly stated that China's Ministry of State Security asked Ms. Huang to provide them with some unspecified information, which she allegedly did in accordance with Chinese law. They also claimed that her husband, businessman Kang Wei, was a Chinese intelligence asset. However, while the full extent of Ms. Huang's relationship with the Chinese government remains unclear, there is reportedly nothing to suggest that she passed on any significant information.

The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Ms. Huang was an intelligence agent. In an Oct. 30 press conference, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun called such reports "unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China." He later reiterated China's stance after Huang revealed his first affair on Nov. 8.

"On the so-called 'Chinese spy,' we have made our position clear," Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning said in a Nov. 12 press briefing. "China's sci-tech progress relies on independent innovation and open cooperation. The U.S. should stop fabricating the 'Chinese spy' narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions."
